source: Wikipedia articles that record a specific event on one atlas island, with an open-licence photograph of the subject

rows.title: The rats ate the meal
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: The island continued to be inhabited until the entire population of thirty died shortly after 1685.
rows.summary: Shortly after 1685 everyone living on North Rona died, about thirty people in all. Black rats had come ashore from a wreck and eaten the stored barley meal. The island's history treats hunger as the likely cause, and allows that plague may have contributed.

rows.title: The last garefowl
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: On Stac an Armin, in July, 1840, the last great auk (Pinguinus impennis) seen in Britain was caught and killed.
rows.summary: In July 1840 the last great auk recorded in Britain was taken on Stac an Armin and killed. Three men from St Kilda caught the bird, which they called a garefowl, and noticed how small its wings were. The stack stands just north of Boreray.

rows.title: Nine months on the stack
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: Three men and eight boys from Hirta were marooned here from about 15 August 1727 until 13 May 1728.
rows.summary: About 15 August 1727, three men and eight boys from Hirta were stranded on Stac an Armin. Smallpox on Hirta meant no one could put a boat out to fetch them. They remained on the stack until 13 May 1728.

rows.title: Left on the rock
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: He rowed out to the rock one night at low tide and left his wife stranded on the rock to die.
rows.summary: In 1527 Lachlan Maclean of Duart took his wife, Catherine Campbell, out to Lady's Rock at low tide and left her there. The skerry goes under at high water. A passing boat lifted her off during the night, so the rock was empty when he looked again the next day.

rows.title: The tanker at the jetty
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: The oil tanker Betelgeuse exploded in Bantry Bay, at the offshore jetty for the oil terminal at Whiddy Island.
rows.summary: Around one in the morning on 8 January 1979 the tanker Betelgeuse exploded at the offshore jetty of the oil terminal on Whiddy Island. The ship was discharging crude oil when the hull failed. Fifty people were killed.

rows.image_alt: The disused tanker jetty at Whiddy Island

rows.title: The row from the lighthouse
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: In the early hours of 7 September 1838, Darling, looking from an upstairs window, spotted the wreck and survivors of the Forfarshire on Big Harcar, a nearby low, rocky island.
rows.summary: In the early hours of 7 September 1838 the steamer Forfarshire broke apart on Big Harcar, the rock next to Longstone. From the Longstone lighthouse, Grace Darling saw survivors still on the wreck. She and her father, the keeper, rowed the lighthouse boat across and brought them off.

rows.title: The raid in June
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: In 793, a Viking raid on Lindisfarne caused consternation throughout the Christian west, and is often taken as the beginning of the Viking Age.
rows.summary: In 793 raiders attacked the monastery on Lindisfarne, and the shock was felt across Christian Europe. The island's chronicle is read as dating the attack to 8 June. Monks were killed and others were taken. The raid is often counted as the start of the Viking Age in Britain.

rows.title: A ward for plague ships
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: St Helen's Isolation hospital, also known as the Pest House, was a quarantine station built in 1764 to house plague cases from visiting ships calling at Old Grimsby and St Helen's Pool.
rows.summary: In 1764 a quarantine hospital, called the Pest House, was built on St Helen's in Scilly. Parliament had ordered in 1754 that a plague ship north of Cape Finisterre and bound for England must anchor off the island. A slip and a quay were added so the sick could be landed.

rows.title: The conductor torn out
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: In the first year of operation, the copper lightning conductor was wrenched out of its sockets by a storm at a height of 92 feet (28 m) above high water.
rows.summary: The light on Dubh Artach, the rock west of Mull, was finished in 1872. In its first year a storm ripped the copper lightning conductor out of the tower. The metal was pulled from its fixings about 92 feet above high water.

rows.title: The first yacht club
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: The world's first yacht club was founded on Haulbowline in 1720.
rows.summary: In 1720 a yacht club was started on Haulbowline, in Cork Harbour. The island's history calls it the first in the world. The west side of the island is now the base of the Irish Naval Service.

rows.title: Twenty-six years a prisoner
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: Edwin Lindsay, an Indian army officer and the son of the 6th Earl of Balcarres, was declared insane and sent to the island in disgrace after refusing to fight in one.
rows.summary: Edwin Lindsay, an army officer and a son of the Earl of Balcarres, was declared insane after he refused a duel and was sent to Papa Stour. He was held on the island as a prisoner for 26 years. A Quaker preacher, Catherine Watson, arranged his release in 1835.

rows.title: Broken in the fog
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: The Hastings County, a 116-metre Norwegian cargo ship, ran ashore on north west of Auskerry in 1926 during thick fog.
rows.summary: In 1926 the Norwegian freighter Hastings County, 116 metres long, ran onto the north-west of Auskerry in thick fog. The ship broke in half. The engine and other wreckage were left on the beach.

rows.title: Caught by the tide
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: In 2011, a Daniel Defoe of Livingston, West Lothian and an unidentified female found themselves trapped on the island due to miscalculating the times of the tide.
rows.summary: In 2011 two people were cut off on Cramond Island after they misread the tide that covers the causeway. One of them was a man from Livingston named Daniel Defoe. The name, shared with the author of Robinson Crusoe, is what turned a stranding into a news story.

rows.title: Everyone left together
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: The evacuation of the community from Inistrahull took place en bloc in 1929.
rows.summary: In 1929 the resident community of Inishtrahull left the island all at once. The departure was raised in the Dáil that November. Keepers remained at the lighthouse until the light was automated in April 1987.

rows.title: The hut was the target
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: A hut was built on the island in 1820 as a shelter for fishermen and sailors at the instigation of John Le Mesurier (hereditary governor of Alderney), but was destroyed during the German occupation of the Channel Islands (the Wehrmacht used it for target practice during WWII).
rows.summary: A shelter for fishermen and sailors was built on Burhou in 1820. During the occupation of the Channel Islands, German forces used the hut as a target and destroyed it. A new hut was put up in 1953.

rows.title: A mine by Boat Cave
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: In 1945, a mine exploded near Boat Cave, causing damage to the cliff face, which is still visible.
rows.reject_reason: The photograph is Fingal's Cave. The Staffa article places the 1945 explosion at Boat Cave, and the summary itself says that cave is away from Fingal's Cave. The picture is not the place of the event.
rows.summary: In 1945 a mine exploded in the sea beside Boat Cave, on the south-west of Staffa. The blast scarred the cliff, and the mark is still there. Boat Cave lies next to Mackinnon's Cave, away from Fingal's Cave.

rows.title: Burned after the siege
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: The castle was besieged then burned by the Covenanters under General Leslie in 1647 during the Wars of the Three Kingdoms.
rows.summary: Gylen Castle stands on a headland at the south end of Kerrera. In 1647 Covenanter soldiers under General Leslie besieged the tower and burned it. The MacDougalls had built it in 1582, and it had been lived in for only a short time.
